title: machine server9p leaks ~8 handles per file op (Hyper-V), host kernel memory grows unbounded
body:
### Issue Description

`podman machine server9p` (the Hyper-V 9p share server, child of `podman machine start`) leaks Windows handles linearly with 9p file operations: ~8.2 handles per file op, measured twice. The leaked handles live in kernel memory, so Task Manager shows nothing per-process while host RAM fills up (~12 GB unaccounted outside all process working sets on a 29 GB box, Memory Compression growing, performance counters failing with c0000bb8).

Observed on a freshly restarted machine (clean server9p at ~300 handles):
- After one job doing ~63k file ops (create + read 3000 small files x20 sweeps under the 9p bind): 520 -> 516,790 handles.
- After a second identical job (~63k ops): 516,790 -> 1,032,992 handles.

The server9p process also survives `podman machine stop` (had to be killed by PID), and a stale gvproxy likewise survived and blocked the next `machine start` until killed.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Windows 11 host, `podman machine init` + `start` (HyperV provider, 8 CPU / 2 GiB / 100 GiB), Podman 6.1.4, no Podman Desktop.
2. Note baseline: `Get-Process podman | Select-Object Name,Id,Handles` (the `server9p --serve ...` process).
3. Run a container workload with many small file ops on the 9p bind, e.g.:
   `mkdir -p /work/synth && for i in $(seq 1 3000); do printf '...' > /work/synth/f$i.txt; done` then `cat /work/synth/*.txt > /dev/null` x20.
4. Re-check handles: grows ~8 per file op, never released. Repeat: linear again.

### Describe the results you received

Handle count grows ~8.2 per file operation, monotonically, across jobs (520 -> 516,790 -> 1,032,992). Host physical memory fills with no corresponding process growth (~12 GB outside all working sets); only symptom is Memory Compression + swap churn.

### Describe the results you expected

Handle count stable across jobs; per-operation handles released when each 9p op completes.

### podman info output

```yaml

  APIVersion: 6.1.4
  GitCommit: 464c15fec06f0074c916f9eff87c4806869c2833
  GoVersion: go1.26.8
  Os: windows
  OsArch: windows/amd64
  Version: 6.1.4
host:
  arch: amd64
  cpus: 8
  distribution:
    distribution: fedora
    variant: podman-machine-os
  memFree: 1980481536
  memTotal: 2116026368
  vmType: hyperv
version:
  APIVersion: 6.1.4
  GoVersion: go1.26.9-X:nodwarf5
  Os: linux
  OsArch: linux/amd64
  Version: 6.1.4
```

(Full 160-line `podman info` on file; host/guest identity trimmed to the fields above. Complete output available on request.)

### Podman in a container

No

### Privileged Or Rootless

_No response_

### Upstream Latest Release

Yes

### Additional environment details

Windows 11 Pro 25H2 (build 26200), Hyper-V provider, machine 8 CPU / 2 GiB / 100 GiB, default 9p shares, no Podman Desktop involved.

### Additional information

- Repro uses default container flags (no --privileged); the leak is in the host-side 9p server, not in container privilege mode.
- The leak does not affect 9p throughput itself (measured ~1.85ms/file clean vs ~1.3ms/file pre-restart — same order); it only eats host kernel memory over time, which makes it easy to misattribute to the workload.
- Related but different mechanism: #25974 (Go-heap OOM in podman-remote during pull) — this one is kernel handles in server9p, no heap growth, no pull involved.

comments.body:
Update with more data points (same machine, fresh server9p after a restart, Podman 6.1.4, Hyper-V 8CPU/2GiB):

- 3k creates + 15k reads + 15k stats in one job: +261k handles (~7.9/op blended).
- creates-only (3k files): +21k handles (~7.0/create).
- 10k scale, one job: creates 26s, 5x10k reads 36s, 5x10k stats 34s; +647k handles over ~60k file ops (~10.7/op).

Two notes: (1) per-file read/stat latency actually drops with scale here (guest page cache warming: ~0.7ms/read at 10k vs ~2.3ms at 3k), while the handle leak stays linear — so throughput and leak are independent issues. (2) I attempted a per-op-type split (create vs read vs stat) but host-side sampling cannot align atomically with step edges, so I am not claiming per-type rates; the aggregate ~8-10 handles per file op across 5 jobs is the solid number.
